I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00932

“I then saw how far I had strayed from the path of Truth: I was heading straight down the road to ruin and unbelief. So I spoke privately with my God, asking Him to deliver me from it all. And there arose within me, taking possession of my whole being, a longing to renounce everything and to be alone; a desire to turn toward God by entering the path of tawhîd, the realization of divine unity.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00933

“But I knew that this would be impossible as long as I remained among kings, in my familiar native land, in the company of my brothers and friends. I understood that it would be better to renounce them, to leave them behind, and to go somewhere that would give me every possible help in living a life worthy of the name. So I abandoned family and fortune, king and honors, father and mother, brothers, close friends, and companions.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00934

Stripping himself of everything, our pilgrim kept only an old, discarded khirqa, a Sufi cloak, and set out to visit the Shiite holy places, then Jerusalem, and finally the sanctuary at Mecca. His route took him through Qazwîn and Ray and back to Isfahan, where, not long before, he had spent so much time enjoying the pleasures of a privileged youth.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00935

Now he associated only with Sufis, entering into a pact of spiritual brotherhood (fotowwat) with them. He placed himself especially under the guidance of a shaykh named Nûroddin Tehrânî. “This shaykh was a great mystic, an ascetic acknowledged by the entire spiritual elite...” Alas, it is in the middle of this unfinished sentence that autobiography A abruptly breaks off, leaving us little hope of finding its continuation elsewhere.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00936

For the moment, we can learn nothing more about our Sayyed’s spiritual experiences in Isfahan, apart from two dreams to which we shall return. It is autobiography B, which takes up the story after his decisive choice of voluntary exile, that tells us about Haydar’s work and literary output during the second period of his life.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00937

This marks the beginning of his Iraqi period, or more precisely its first phase (period B). Sayyed Haydar travelled to Mecca and Medina, where he would have liked to settle. He dates this pilgrimage to 751 AH (1350–51 CE). Ill health, however, forced him to return to Iraq and its Shiite holy places. Since the Treatise on the Knowledge of Being is dated at Najaf in 768 AH (1366–67 CE), we shall use that work as our point of reference for distinguishing the second phase of his Iraqi period (period C), at least as far as his writings are concerned.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00938

As for the first phase, the biographical accounts tell us that in Baghdad Sayyed Haydar studied under two eminent shaykhs: Mawlânâ Nasîroddin Kashânî Hillî (d. 755/1354) and the shaykh commonly known as Fakhr al-Mohaqqiqîn (682/1283–771/1370), son of the celebrated ’Allâmeh Hillî (648/1250–726/1326). The latter had himself studied under Nasîroddin Tûsî and Kâtibî Qazwînî and was one of the leading figures in Shiite theology at the time.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00939

In 761 AH (1359–60 CE), Fakhr al-Mohaqqiqîn granted Sayyed Haydar an ijâzat, an authorization to teach the books he had studied with him. It was at this teacher’s request that Haydar wrote the Risâlat raf’ât al-khilâf, a treatise defending the First Shiite Imam’s conduct toward the first three caliphs recognized by Sunnism; the two men also exchanged a number of questions and answers. Beyond this, the only reliable information presently available comes from our Sayyed himself, in autobiography B and in the account of his own writings.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00940

Let us recall that the latest date we can establish is that of his Treatise on the Higher Sciences, written in 787 AH (1385–86 CE). Sayyed Haydar was then sixty-five years old, or sixty-seven by the lunar calendar. After that, all trace of him disappears. We know neither when nor under what circumstances he died.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00941

As already noted, autobiography B appears in the introduction to Haydar’s great commentary on Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs al-hikam, completed in 782 AH (1380–81 CE). He was then sixty-two lunar years old and had been away from his native Iran for thirty-two years. Here is what he writes:
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00942

“When God Most High commanded me to renounce everything other than Him and to turn toward Him in true conversion, He inspired me to seek a place, a dwelling where I could settle and devote myself to serving and worshipping Him, as His command and guidance required—a place beyond which there would be none higher or more illustrious in this world.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00943

“And so I set out for Mecca—may God Most High exalt it—after renouncing my office as minister, power, wealth, honors, my father and mother, my brothers and companions. I put on an old, worthless khirqa that had been thrown away and left my native country, Âmol and Tabarestan, toward Khorasan.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00944

“There I had been the minister (vazîr) of the ruler of the country, one of the most illustrious sovereigns of Persia, for he was among the august descendants of Kesrâ [Khosrow]. His name was al-Malik al-Sa’îd Fakhroddawleh, son of the late king Shâh Katkhodâ—may God grant them both a dwelling in Paradise. I was thirty years old at that time.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00945
“In this way, until the moment I reached Mecca, I had to face trials of every kind and struggles of every sort. It would take several volumes to tell the whole story.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00946

“Yet in most of the circumstances I passed through, I found myself repeating these words of God: ‘Whoever leaves his home to migrate toward God and His Messenger and is overtaken by death—his reward is surely with God; and God is forgiving and merciful’ (4:151). Or, in the words of a gnostic whose ardent longing resembled my own: ‘For Your pleasure I have renounced all creatures; / I have made orphans of my own people so that I might behold You. / Even if You cut me limb from limb, / My heart would yearn for no one but You.’
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00947

“In short, this was my condition until I reached Mecca. There I performed the obligatory pilgrimage and carried out the prescribed rites, together with the voluntary acts of devotion and the other observances. This was in the year 751 of the Hijra (1350–51 CE). I had intended to settle there, but then an ardent desire arose within me to make my home in Medina, for I had not yet paid my visit—my pilgrimage of devotion—to the Messenger of God, his descendants, and his companions.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00948
“So I made my way to Medina. I visited the Messenger of God and resolved to remain there.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00949

“But obstacles once again intervened, first of all physical illness, until I had no choice but to return to Iraq, to that familiar place, the magnificent and most sacred shrine at Najaf—may God’s peace be upon the one who gives it its glory [Imam ’Alî].
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00950

“I returned there in health and settled permanently, devoting myself entirely to spiritual exercises and retreat, to worship and the service of God, with a breadth, fervor, and seriousness beyond which it would scarcely have been possible to go. Then, during this period, from God and His suprasensible Presences, there flowed into my heart the spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl) of the Quran and the commentary on the Fosûs that I have already mentioned: a whole world of ideas and higher knowledge, truths and subtle perceptions, which it is impossible to set out in detail in any way, because these are the Words of God (Kalimât Allâh), which can neither be counted nor brought to an end nor interrupted.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00951

This long passage does more than acquaint us with the outward setting and chronology of a spiritual adventure. It lets us glimpse the man’s secret: the personal, inward rule of his life, unbending and reducible to no other. A restrained emotion runs through it, revealing the gifts that made Haydar Âmolî the man he was.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00952

Among the qualities that most clearly mark his personality, we must also single out the vitality of his active imagination: his ability to perceive the suprasensible world on the plane of the imaginal world (’âlam al-mithâl). This faculty reaches the level of visionary perception, sometimes in dreams, sometimes in an intermediate state between waking and sleeping. Haydar Âmolî has left us accounts of several dreams and visions, including two dreams he had in Isfahan while passing through the city on the great journey that took him from his native Tabarestan toward the Shiite holy places.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00953

“Know that I was travelling, and my route took me through Isfahan. I was bound for Baghdad, to visit the holy places of the Imams and to make the pilgrimage to the most sacred sanctuary at Mecca, both to fulfill a religious obligation and with the intention of settling there. Then, one night, I had the following dream-vision: I found myself in the cloth merchants’ market in Isfahan.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00954

“I was looking at my own body lying full-length on the ground. It was dead, wrapped in a white shroud, while I stood gazing at it with curiosity, amazed by my predicament: how could I be standing there, and at the same time be a dead man lying on the ground? I remained in this condition until I awoke.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00955

“On another occasion, also in a dream in Isfahan, I was leaning against the shop of a certain companion... On my shoulders was a gilded pewter vessel, like those carried by some of the water sellers who move among the people offering them a drink... And I was giving water to those present, all the while observing myself with curiosity.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00956

Both dreams give a characteristic picture of our Sayyed’s inner condition after he had decisively broken with the youth still so close behind him and given himself entirely to divine service. In his dreams he thus gives visible form to an experience well known in the psychology of mysticism: the spiritual birth of a new person.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00957

We possess other accounts of his visions, notably one of the night sky above Baghdad, in which he saw—whether dreaming or in an intermediate state he does not say—a blazing diagram embodying all his Shiite devotion: the names of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones written in letters of fire within circles of lapis lazuli, arranged as an immense quadrilateral across the starry sky (see § 5 below).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00958

To the extent that it is true to say each person is what they love, and that we can therefore understand someone only through their love—through everything that gave their life its purpose and meaning—Haydar Âmolî’s dreams, like those of his fellow mystics (a Rûzbehân, a Shams Lâhîjî, a Mîr Dâmâd, and others), must be interpreted together with his work, to which he entrusted his deepest purpose. And Haydar Âmolî’s purpose, the one to which he gave all the strength of his love because it was the very expression of that love, is perfectly clear. We have sketched it above.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00959
Let us now draw out its implications, by way of introduction to the pages in which he will explain it himself.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00960

Sayyed Haydar is an Imami Shiite for whom Shiism represents Islam in its fullness and also Islam’s inner, esoteric dimension. It represents Islam in its fullness because it rests on three things at once: the sharî’at (the outward religion and its law), the tarîqat (the spiritual path), and the haqîqat (the realization of spiritual truth). It is Islam’s esoteric dimension because the haqîqat is the inner truth of the sharî’at, just as the sharî’at is its outward form, and because the holy Imams are both the keepers of this hidden truth and the truth they keep—both its bestowers and its substance.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00961

Yet the situation Haydar faces is this: Shiites condemn Sufis, and Sufis condemn Shiites. In doing so, the Shiites confine themselves to the sharî’at alone, the outward religion, while the Sufis forget where their khirqa—the cloak symbolizing their spiritual initiation—came from, and thus leave the haqîqat, the inward religion, hanging in midair.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00962

Both sides make the same mistake when they act as if the teaching of the holy Imams had nothing to do with the higher spiritual sciences, when it was the Imams who first taught them. The tested believer (mu’min momtahan) is the one who embraces the Imams’ cause and teaching in their entirety, holding together sharî’at, tarîqat, and haqîqat. This is why, beside a Shiite who stops at the sharî’at, it is the Sufi who is the true Shiite.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00963
But beside a Sufi who rejects religious law or forgets the origins of his khirqa, it is the Shiite who embraces the whole teaching who is the true Sufi.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00964

Thus the whole effort of Haydar Âmolî’s great Jâmi’ al-asrâr is directed toward persuading the two groups, Shiites and Sufis, that neither can do without the other. Its central proposition is this: the true Shiites are the Sufis—a claim whose meaning emerges fully only when it is reversed: the true Sufis are the true Shiites. We should read the book’s opening and conclusion together (see § 3 below), for these passages reveal our Sayyed’s character better than any other account. In opening up the spiritual world to which he bears witness, they also show us the importance and the courage of his undertaking.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00965
Elsewhere in the book, too, there are moments when the secret of his inner life suddenly shines through. Here is one:
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00966

“You should know that our purpose in conducting this discussion with you and with others is neither fanatical zeal nor controversy—God preserve us from such things! No, our aim is to bring harmony between the two sides and to lead each of you toward the truth that is yours... Otherwise, through God’s care and the excellence of His help, I myself put such things behind me long ago. For twenty years I have witnessed the situation as it really is, as I mentioned in the introduction to this book.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00967

“I have been delivered from that darkness and have emerged from those depths: the darkness of contention and controversy, the depths of fanaticism and argument. And for this I give glory to God... In this state of mine, I recite a poem written by someone before me, because it expresses my own experience perfectly; these are the lines I so often find myself repeating: ‘I love You with two loves: a love of passion, / And a love of which You alone are worthy...’”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00968

Passages like these make one long to see all of Sayyed Haydar Âmolî’s writings brought to light. The discovery of his autobiography has enabled us to identify almost all their titles: thirty-four, as we have said, to which we may cautiously add three or four more mentioned by bibliographers. Unfortunately, of this vast body of work we have so far been able to discover manuscripts of only six.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00969

Admittedly, the author’s own statements make it clear that these six are his most important works, and publishing them alone would require some twenty volumes in the usual octavo format. A systematic, chronological inventory of our Sayyed’s bibliography has already appeared elsewhere, in the introductions to the first published volume of his writings. There is no need to repeat it in detail here.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00970
We shall concentrate on just four works of major importance.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00971

The Jâmi’ al-asrâr wa manba’ al-anwâr, literally The Sum of Esoteric Teachings and the Source of Lights. Asrâr means “secrets”: hidden, inward, esoteric realities disclosed through the act of knowing called kashf—inner unveiling, mystical intuition, visionary perception. Taken together, these realities constitute theosophy, or wisdom grounded in spiritual insight, whereas rational understanding (’aql) is the instrument of philosophy, and transmitted tradition (naql) provides the material of theology. This is the great treatise already mentioned, from whose opening and conclusion we shall read several passages below. It was written early in Haydar’s Iraqi period (period B), around 752 AH (1351–52 CE). We have already described its central purpose; let us add that it contains many autobiographical allusions. It consists of three books, each called an asl (source or principle), and each book is divided into four major chapters, or qâ’ida (foundational teaching). The structure of the work is thus organized around the number twelve.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00972

Book I sets out the essence and truth of tawhîd, the affirmation and realization of divine unity. It establishes the distinction between theological tawhîd (olâhî, outward or exoteric monotheism) and ontological or esoteric tawhîd (tawhîd wojûdî), which affirms the transcendent unity of being (wahdat al-wojûd)—not some supposed “existential monism.” The author shows that theological tawhîd can conceal a shirk, a hidden dualism or unconscious idolatry. Ontological tawhîd is then presented in terms of Ibn ’Arabî’s metaphysics.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00973

Finally, Haydar links the argument to a spiritual interpretation of Quran 33:72, from which it emerges that the burden accepted by the human being in an act of sublime madness is nothing less than the secret of the Imams. They themselves repeatedly said that their cause is so difficult and so heavy that only an angel, a prophet, or a believer whose heart has been tested can bear it. This provides the basis for affirming that Sufis, insofar as they claim the gnosis handed down from the Imams, are the “Shiites in the true sense”; conversely, those Shiites who accept the entirety of the holy Imams’ teaching are “believers whose hearts have been tested,” and therefore Sufis in the true sense.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00974

Book II carries this argument forward by assembling the evidence in sequence: Quranic verses, sayings of the Prophet, sayings of the holy Imams, and teachings of the great spiritual masters (the Mashâyekh).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00975

Book III is perfectly symmetrical. Each of its four chapters deals with three fundamental concepts in Shiite theosophy, arranging the terms so that their corresponding places within each triad become clear.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00976

The four triads are: 1) the outward, literal religion (sharî’at), the mystical path (tarîqat), and the truth of gnosis and spiritual realization (haqîqat); 2) the prophetic message (risâlat), the prophetic vocation (nobowwat), and the Imam’s walâyat—his standing as Walî Allâh, Friend of God and guide of spiritual initiation; 3) revelation or divine communication through the Angel (wahy), inspiration (ilhâm), and inward unveiling (kashf, mystical intuition or sacred knowledge received through vision); 4) islâm (the act of surrendering oneself to God), îmân (faith understood as fidelity in the Shiite sense, requiring the heart’s assent to a threefold testimony: divine unity, the Prophet’s mission, and the walâyat of the Imams), and îqân (certainty that is at once pistis, faith, and gnôsis, knowledge).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00977

The chapter on prophecy and walâyat is especially extensive. Here Haydar Âmolî argues against Ibn ’Arabî that it is impossible, both historically and in the structure of the doctrine, to regard Jesus son of Mary as the “Seal” of absolute walâyat, or to accept, as certain of Ibn ’Arabî’s disciples did, that Ibn ’Arabî himself was the Seal of particular, or Muhammadan, walâyat. The Seal of absolute walâyat can only be the First Imam; the Seal of Muhammadan walâyat can only be the figure whom Twelver Shiism recognizes as the Twelfth Imam: the presently Hidden Imam, the awaited Mahdi, son of Imam Hasan ’Askarî.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00978

Haydar will develop this argument at even greater length some thirty years later, in the introduction to his commentary on Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs. By following through all the implications of the doctrine that walâyat is the inward truth of prophecy, Haydar Âmolî’s work marks a major moment in the development of “prophetic philosophy” within Shiite Islam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00979

The Treatise on the Knowledge of Being (Risâlat fî ma’rifat al-wojûd), completed in Najaf on 15 Jumada II 768 AH, corresponding to 17 February 1367. This date allows us to distinguish the two phases of our Sayyed’s Iraqi period (periods B and C). He wrote the treatise at the request of a friend whom he does not name, but for whom he felt deep affection. It is a summary—quite a substantial one, despite the author’s description—of a much larger work on metaphysics, of which no manuscript has yet been found. Sayyed Haydar tells us that he had just completed a major treatise examining every aspect of being, explaining the disagreement between the Motakallimûn, the scholastic theologians, and the philosophers who profess the transcendent unity of being, and bringing forward testimony from the Word of God and the words of the prophets and the Awliyâ, God’s Friends. At that point, he writes, “one of my brothers, dearer to me than the pupils of my eyes, earnestly asked me to make a concise and useful summary of it: a book small in size but rich in instruction.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00980

Like the larger work it condenses, the treatise has an introduction and three “pillars” (rokn), or chapters. They deal, respectively, with: 1) the problem of being (status quaestionis): being understood as absolute being (itlāq al-wojûd) and being as something immediately given. Here Haydar stresses the impossibility of deducing being, of deriving it rationally through a principle of sufficient reason.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00981

This leads to the question of tarjîh: why does being prevail over nonbeing? Why is there something rather than nothing? 2) The necessity of being and its unity. 3) The manifestation of being (zohûr al-wojûd) and its multiplicity. From the outset (§ 5), the author explains that he approaches the metaphysics of being from three perspectives: that of the philosophers, through intellect (’aql); that of the theologians, through tradition (naql); and that of the mystical theosophers, through intuitive perception (kashf). This is wholly consistent with his characteristic position and with the method employed in his great Jâmi’ al-asrâr.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00982

Thus, when announcing his book’s title, Sayyed Haydar dedicates it to those who possess the necessary readiness, the full capacity, the subtlety and penetration the subject requires. He excludes those who deny and dispute, all who stand far from God and the Friends of God.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00983

We hardly need emphasize the importance of works like these for the history of Islamic philosophy, which historians long supposed had come to an end with Averroes in Andalusia. Haydar Âmolî approaches the metaphysics of being neither as Avicenna did nor as Averroes did.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00984

Yet he confronts precisely the same problem inherited from Greek philosophy. What differs is his manner of confronting it, and the resources he brings to bear: his profound knowledge of Ibn ’Arabî’s writings, his ceaseless meditation on the Book of God, and his study of the traditions of the Shiite Imams. It would be inconceivable to him, as to the Shiite philosophers we are studying, that anyone should try to develop a metaphysics of being while accepting the division, so common in the West, that isolates philosophy from theology.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00985

To insist on keeping the two apart is to mutilate the questions—and the intellectual aims—of both. It blocks the passage through which each, by way of the other, can reach the higher plane of theosophical metaphysics. The result is the absurd position in which some people deny that our philosophers are dealing with philosophical questions at all, when it would be simpler and more “objective” to acknowledge that their understanding of philosophy extends beyond the limits imposed on the word by “modern” philosophy.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00986

Haydar Âmolî and thinkers like him have much in common with the Neoplatonic theosophers of the European Renaissance. It is as a Neoplatonist that Sayyed Haydar meditates on the threefold structure of the bismillâh: Allâh signifies the absolute One, oneness in its most absolute sense (ahadîya); al-Rahmân, the Merciful, signifies the One as multiple, the Nous or divine Intellect, the Imam or metaphysical Adam; and al-Rahîm, the Most Compassionate, signifies the World Soul, the metaphysical Eve.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00987

The Shiite philosophy that Haydar Âmolî sought to present in its fullness would be developed still further by Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, and several others. It is of exceptional interest, as we see it, for the study of religious consciousness as it is experienced.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00988

The two works just discussed have recently been published. We must now mention two further works of central importance, both immense in scope, about which we have already said something. The first is the Tafsîr ’irfânî, Haydar’s monumental spiritual and mystical commentary on the Quran, completed in 777 AH (1375–76 CE). It fills seven large volumes, preserved in the author’s own manuscript, whose recent discovery at Najaf and Qomm we have described above. This tafsîr, or Quranic commentary, bears an elaborate, symbolically charged title. Haydar Âmolî explains it as follows when he refers to his earlier writings in the introduction to his commentary on Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00989

“Our own books fall into two categories: those that have been poured down upon us from above, and those that have proceeded from ourselves. Those poured down upon us from above are the ta’wîlât, the spiritual interpretations of the holy Quran. They contain the most precious and exalted divine teachings and Quranic sciences; they gather together the symbols and forms belonging to the Prophet, the subtle teachings and Muhammadan realities faithfully expressed by what God says of the chosen among His servants: ‘I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, what no ear has heard, and what has never entered the heart of any human being.’
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00990

“Accordingly, this book has received the title The Supreme Ocean and the Loftiest Mountain: A Book on the Spiritual Interpretation of the Precious and Unshakeable Book of God (al-Mohît al-a’zam wa’l-tawd al-ashamm fî ta’wîl Kitâb Allâh al-’azîz al-mohkam). Its plan is divided into seven volumes, placing it under the auspices of the seven great prophets, the seven spiritual poles, and the seven abdâl [a rank of hidden spiritual figures].
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00991

“Thus the introductory sections, together with the Fâtiha [the Quran’s opening sura], form one volume, and each successive sixth of the Quran forms another. This tafsîr stands in relation to us as the Fosûs al-hikam stands in relation to Shaykh Mohyiddin Ibn ’Arabî, and as the Quran stands in relation to the Prophet. The structure of our tafsîr is as follows: we begin by establishing nineteen premises and circles, consisting of seven premises and twelve circles, corresponding to the outward world and the spiritual world, to the ‘Book of the Horizons’ and the ‘Book of Souls,’ each of these worlds being bounded by the number nineteen.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00992

Two observations arise here. First, Sayyed Haydar is referring to the way Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs can be regarded as an “inspired book”: according to the account, the Prophet gave it to Ibn ’Arabî in a dream, having himself received it in the Malakût, the spiritual realm. By comparing his own Tafsîr to Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs, our Sayyed illustrates and confirms what he has just said: that the Tafsîr is not a book originating in himself, but one that he knows was “poured down upon him from above.” It came by way of the inspiration that Shiite thought about knowledge holds to remain open even after the cycle of prophecy has closed.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00993

Second, the structure of the Tafsîr’s introductory sections, as Haydar Âmolî describes them, corresponds to the structure of the esoteric hierarchy: seven prophets and twelve Imams, nineteen figures in all. His talk of circles also calls to mind the elaborate diagrams he constructed with such artistry. We have already discussed the meaning of what we propose to call the “diagrammatic art” that illustrates Haydar Âmolî’s writings.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00994

Elsewhere in the same introduction, Sayyed Haydar describes his magnum opus as “divided into seven large volumes, corresponding to the ta’wîl of the eminent shaykh Najmoddin Râzî, known as Dâyéh. For he too divided his work into seven large volumes, having given it the title Ocean of Spiritual Truths and Mystical Realities (Bahr al-haqâ’iq wa’l-daqâ’iq).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00995

“Our intention was to produce a book comparable to his in every respect, and satisfying the hadîth that also underlies his work: ‘The Quran has an outward [exoteric] meaning and an inward [esoteric] meaning; this inward meaning itself has a further inward meaning, and so on down to seven inward depths’ [...]. This tafsîr [that of Najm Dâyéh] is famous in every clime and every country.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00996

“The theosophical truth of its structure is recognized by the most eminent philosophers and mystical theosophers. They acknowledge that it has no equal or parallel, especially in the Quranic sciences, and that it was attained neither by acquiring knowledge from outside nor by prolonged dialectical inquiry, but through a secret gift from the All-Merciful, by means of mystical perception (kashf).”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00997

Sayyed Haydar thus allows us to glimpse at least the plan of his mystical tafsîr and something of the secret of its contents. Until we can study it in detail and prepare an edition, we already know the perspective in which its author places it. By referring to Najm Dâyéh Râzî’s work, Haydar Âmolî is also evoking the whole body of mystical Quran commentaries. This literature is vast. It still awaits systematic classification and study, work that can be undertaken only by scholars trained in philosophy and religious studies.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00998

For their essential interest lies in how the Quran was read by Islam’s spiritual masters and metaphysicians. There is no point in objecting that those thinkers’ methods of interpretation do not conform to the aims or procedures of our own “positive,” historical-critical scholarship. Such an objection would accomplish nothing. As we said above concerning the metaphysics of being, we Western interpreters have no right to impose a supposedly “modern” agenda upon our authors.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00999

Our task is to grasp the meaning of the questions that belonged—or still belong—to the intellectual agenda of these philosophers, and to bring their significance to light. The writings in which this agenda unfolds are immense in scope. Think of the ta’wîlât of Rûzbehân Baqlî Shîrâzî, ’Abdorrazzaq Kâshânî, Sayyed Ahmad ’Alawî, and Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, down to the great mystical tafsîr of Soltân ’Alî-Shâh in the nineteenth century.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01000

We must add that Shiite Quran commentaries as a whole, including Ismaili commentaries, also belong to the tradition of mystical Quranic interpretation—if we understand “mystical” broadly, to include every interpretation that raises or deepens the Quran’s literal wording toward its hidden meaning. That hidden meaning concerns the person of the Imam and embraces all the levels of being at which the metaphysics of the Imams locates him.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01001

It was within this very perspective that our Sayyed’s reference to Najm Dâyéh Râzî confronted us with a difficult problem, one that has left earlier scholars equally uncertain: what exactly is the relationship between three of the most celebrated mystical Quran commentaries, those of Najmoddin Kobrâ (d. 618/1221), Najm Dâyéh Râzî (d. 654/1255), and ’Alâoddawleh Semnânî (d. 736/1336)? Bibliographers make statements on this point that do not always agree.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01002

Without repeating the details of the argument, let us give the conclusions reached by our own research and that of Osman Yahia. Najmoddin Kobrâ did indeed begin a major mystical commentary on the Quran, under the title ’Ayn al-Hayât (The Spring of Life), but he got no farther than the boundary between the fourth and fifth suras. His disciple Najm Dâyéh Râzî undertook to continue it, starting again from the beginning of the Quran under the title Bahr al-haqâ’iq (The Ocean of Spiritual Truths).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01003

Death, however, prevented him from taking his Tafsîr beyond the fifty-third sura, The Star. In turn, ’Alâoddawleh Semnânî resumed the unfinished work and this time carried it through to the end. He prefaced it with introductory studies setting out the foundations and rules of his spiritual interpretation, which we shall need to compare with Haydar Âmolî’s. The result was a masterpiece of radical inward interpretation, to which we shall return later (chapter IV below).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01004

We intend to publish at least the introduction to Haydar Âmolî’s great Tafsîr ’irfânî. We may call this work the great Sum into which our Sayyed poured the depths of his personal thought and spiritual experience, just as he sought to bring together his prophetic metaphysics in the last treatise he wrote, the Treatise on the Higher Sciences, about which we can say no more for the time being. His Tafsîr is a monument of incalculable value for anyone studying or reflecting upon spiritual interpretation across religious traditions: first within Islam, but also across the forms of interpretation developed in the “religions of the Book,” among the Ahl al-Kitâb, the People of the Book.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01005

As we have already observed, the spiritual thinkers of the three great communities of the Abrahamic tradition confronted the same problems through what we might call the “phenomenon of the Holy Book.” They pursued the same quest for the “true meaning”; their approaches to interpretation followed the same horizons. All this is of particular interest because it establishes and develops one dimension of the general theory of interpretation, or hermeneutics—a concept so much discussed today. We have already considered this point at length in Book I of the present work.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01006

Finally, a few words about the other major work by Haydar Âmolî now being prepared for publication, to which we have repeatedly referred: his commentary on Ibn ’Arabî’s Fosûs al-hikam, completed in Baghdad in 782 AH (1380–81 CE), and comprising two substantial volumes. He calls it Text of Texts (nass al-nosûs—the supreme text, the text par excellence), written as a commentary on the Fosûs. The introductory sections alone constitute an entire book, a complete system. Among other things, they contain a fervent tribute to Ibn ’Arabî. Yet they also renew the criticism of him that Haydar had already begun in the Jâmi’ al-asrâr, concerning the grave question of the “Seal of walâyat,” a question decisive for Shiite teachings about the Imams.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01007

Here is a partial translation of the “table of contents” of these introductory sections: 1) A testament recommending the discipline of secrecy (ketmân) concerning the divine sciences, so that they are not disclosed to those unworthy of them. 2) First exposition: the eminence of our Prophet and his superiority over all other beings. 3) Second exposition: the eminence of Shaykh Mohyiddin Ibn ’Arabî and his superiority over the other shaykhs, ancient and recent. 4) Third exposition: the eminence of the prophets, the Messengers, and the Imams; the eminence of the spiritual poles and the abdâl. 5) First pillar (rokn): tawhîd and its esoteric dimensions. 6) Second pillar: absolute being and a deepening of its concept. 7) Third pillar: forms of knowledge, their categories and kinds. 8) First circle: the hidden meaning of being, its hierarchy and its branching forms. 9) Second circle: a deeper understanding of ontological tawhîd. 10) Third circle: the hidden meaning of the bismillâh, and of the letters that compose it and correspond to the structure of the outer and inner worlds... and so on, up to nineteen circles.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01008

The idea of these circles is connected with what we have proposed above to call “diagrammatic art.” Haydar Âmolî carefully constructs numerous diagrams, in which he excels at giving visible form to the architecture of his thought, just as the Ismaili philosophers did in their own way. He made such diagrams for his Treatise on the Higher Sciences, for his great Quranic Tafsîr, and above all for the introductions to his commentary on Ibn ’Arabî.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01009

These alone contain more than thirty diagrams, arranging the figures of Ibn ’Arabî’s esoteric teaching—prophets, Imams, the hierarchy of the Invisible Ones, the twelve spiritual poles, and so forth—according to a Shiite scheme. This “diagrammatic” art is not merely an aid to an ars memorativa, an art of memory such as the Latin scholastics knew and practiced. It also supports an ars interiorativa or ars meditativa: an art of inward realization or meditation, which proceeds by discovering correspondences between the “Book of the Horizons” (the Book of Being) and the “Book of Souls” (the Inner Book).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01010

In general terms, it belongs to the art of the mandala. Haydar Âmolî’s diagrams, often drawn in several colors, guide the viewer into the inner world and, in doing so, make that world present eo ipso—by that very act—within the pure space of the “metaphysical image.” They bear witness to the “inner objectivity” proper to such an image. This is an art that in the West may have reached its fullest expression in Giordano Bruno (see also Book II, chapter VII, § 3 above).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
en-book-4-ch-1-s3
3. Shiism and Sufism
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01011

This is the central theme not only of the Jâmi’ al-asrâr, which we have analyzed above, but of Haydar Âmolî’s thought as a whole. It is therefore a theme we have encountered repeatedly throughout the present work. The best course now is to let the author speak for himself.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01012
We shall read the opening and conclusion of his great Jâmi’ al-asrâr to grasp both its purpose and its tone, interrupting only for brief comments—or rather, brief reminders.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01013
The author first tells us that he undertook the work at the request of a group of friends. He explicitly names four books he had written earlier, gives their titles, and then continues:
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01014

“Several of my virtuous brothers, mystical pilgrims travelling the Path of God out of a desire to please Him, repeatedly urged me to write for them a book that would be a comprehensive Sum. It should contain the whole of divine theosophy (asrâr Allâh), the hidden teachings concerning the prophets (asrâr al-Anbiyâ’), and those concerning the Imams and Friends of God (asrâr al-Awliyâ’).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01015

“Above all, it should contain the theosophy of Tawhîd, divine unity, with its categories, consequences, implications, precepts, and secrets. Such a book should explain its inward truths (haqâ’iq), its subtleties, fine distinctions, and symbols; reveal its heart and essence, its sources and the truths derived from them; and trace its ramifications, ambiguities, doubts, and sophistries. Its plan should show the supreme place of Tawhîd: how it is defined, how many forms it takes, and how it is realized. It should offer vivid examples drawn from things the senses can grasp, and clear, compelling testimony.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01016

“Finally, the book should rest on the teaching of the spiritual people (Ahl Allâh) who affirm Unity in its true meaning, those known as Sufis, while remaining in agreement with Twelver Imami Shiism. It should therefore harmonize the principles of Shiism and Sufism, together with everything those principles presuppose, so that every dispute between Shiites and Sufis might be brought to a definitive end, with no need for another book after this one to settle the matter.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01017

“For among all the branches of Islam and the various communities that follow Muhammad, no group has denounced the Sufis as fiercely as the Shiites have; and, conversely, no group has denounced the Shiites as fiercely as the Sufis have.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01018

“Yet both have the same origin, drink from the same source, and refer back to one and the same authority. For the authority to whom all Shiites appeal, especially the Twelver Imamis, is none other than the Commander of the Faithful [the First Imam, ’Alî], followed by his children and his children’s children [the other eleven Imams]. He is the source from which they spring and from which they drink. Their knowledge rests on him, and their fundamental principles refer back to him.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01019

“The same is true of the authentic Sufis (al-sûfiyat al-haqqa), because the one upon whom they base their knowledge, and to whom they trace their spiritual investiture—their khirqa, their Sufi cloak—is none other than the First Imam, followed in succession by his children and his children’s children.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01020

“Indeed, they trace their origin either to Komayl ibn Ziyâd al-Nakha’î, the Imam’s intimate pupil and chosen disciple; or to Hasan Basrî (d. 110/728), likewise one of the Imam’s most eminent pupils and greatest disciples; or to [the Sixth Imam] Ja’far ibn Mohammad al-Sâdiq, a descendant of the First Imam’s descendants, who succeeded him in turn as his spiritual heir, an immaculate Imam (ma’sûm) invested with authority by God.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01021
“We shall show in detail how all this stands in the course of the present book, in shâ’a ’Llâh—God willing.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01022

“The reason I believe these spiritual brothers pressed their request upon me so insistently is that perhaps, with the penetrating eye of their inner vision, they perceived in me the traces of God’s favors and kindnesses, through which He had granted me these mystical and theosophical forms of knowledge (ma’ârif wa haqâ’iq).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01023

“Guided by their spiritual discernment, they recognized the lights of His outpouring and of His self-manifestations (tajalliyât), just as such lights can be recognized when He grants a soul these realities beyond the senses and these subtle things. They saw that I had understood the starting points and fundamental theses of both groups, Shiites and Sufis. And they recognized the excellence of the way these teachings had come together in my own person (majmû’îyatî), because I had made the axioms and conclusions of both schools my own.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01024

“For from the flower of my youth—or rather, from the days of my childhood—down to the present days of my maturity, I have devoted myself, with divine help and assistance, to making my own the fundamental teachings of my forefathers, the holy Imams, and their spiritual path (tarîqat). I have studied them both according to their outward meaning (zâhir), the literal religion (sharî’at) practiced by Imami Shiites among the various branches of Islam, and according to their inward meaning (bâtin), the spiritual truth (haqîqat) to which the Sufis devote themselves, these masters of Tawhîd and people of God.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01025

“I have considered the agreement and harmony of the two so thoroughly that I became aware of what each could rightfully claim. I understood the spiritual truth of each position and brought them into accord, as one sandal matches the other, or as each feather on an arrow is paired with the feather opposite it.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01026

“I thus reached the state in which I now find myself: holding together within myself the literal religion and the truth known through gnosis, embracing the outward and the inward, attaining a plane of equilibrium and stability. I can now receive within myself what is said by all those who have reached a like condition: those who have lived their certainty (arbâb al-yaqîn), those whose knowledge rests upon personal experience (ahl al-tahqîq).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01027

“‘Glory be to God, who has guided us to this. We would never have found guidance had He not Himself guided us’ (7:42). Verse: ‘My heart once harbored many passions; the sieve of Your identity has gathered them into a single passion. Now the one I envied has come to envy me; I became the lord of men when You became my lord. I have left other people their homelands and their faiths, occupied only with the thought of You—You who are my homeland and my faith.’
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01028

“This is no empty boast or wild extravagance, but an account of divine favors and graces, in accordance with His words: ‘As for your Lord’s blessings, speak of them’ (93:11). I do nothing but remember divine generosity and its blessings, in accordance with His words: ‘Do not cease to remind, for remembrance bears fruit among the believers’ (51:55).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01029

“Yet all the many things I have recounted in this book and in others like it, however often I have returned to them, are no more than a grain of sand beside a mountain, or a drop of water beside the Ocean...”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01030

(The author develops this comparison at length, speaking of the secrets of the Jabarût [the realm of divine power], the hidden mysteries of the Malakût [the spiritual realm], and the esoteric truths which the Quran calls the Words of God, words that neither come to an end nor run dry (18:109), and which he has been permitted to know. He then returns to his central concern.)
